text_joined_original: “This is a story about a cowherd and a weaver girl. Originally, the two did not know each other, and were very efficient workers. The boy herded cows well, and the girl wove nice cloth; both did very good work. One day, they met, and fell in love. Soon, they were always playing together and neglecting their work. This made the gods very angry because they forgot about their responsibilities. The gods decided to punish them and cast them away to opposite sides of the Milky Way. Although the gods were angry, they pitied the young lovers and allowed them to meet once a year. When the sparrows lined up along the sky to form a bridge, on July 7 of every [lunar calendar] year, the lovers would be able to meet. This day is called “chi shi ( in Chinese; it means “night of seven.” And this is the origin of Chinese Valentine’s Day, which is on July 7th of the lunar calendar.”

text_joined_original: When I was losing my baby teeth, my mother showed me a way of disposing of the fallen teeth so that my new teeth would grow out properly. If it was teeth of the upper gums, she had me stand with my feet straight and together (so that the teeth will grow out that way) and then throw the tooth downward, usually under the bed. For teeth of the lower jaw, I threw them upward, usually onto a high closet. Throwing teeth up will ensure that the new teeth will grow upward; throwing down would make them grow downwards from the upper jaw.

text_joined_original: Sticks This game is played with 2 or more players. The object of sticks is to get as many sticks as you can without causing any part of the pile of sticks to move. A number of sticks, usually small twigs, are found and collected. One player chooses to handle the pile of sticks, and another player volunteers to have the first turn. Every player then sits in a circle. Everyone chooses one stick from the pile collected. The player that chooses to be the handler of sticks drops the rest of the sticks and allows them to fall in a pile. The player that volunteers to have the first turn will use his stick to try and get a stick from the pile without moving any of the other sticks. If the player succeeds in getting a stick without moving the other sticks, he is allowed to keep his stick. The next turn is the player to the left. The game ends when someone moves the other sticks when trying to get another stick from the pile. The player with the most sticks wins.

label: collection_context
text_joined_original: I learned this superstition from my mother, an American-born Filipino, when I was a child cir­ ca 1977 in Stockton, CA. When a spoon was accidentally dropped someone would say that a woman is coming over and usually laugh afterwards. The same goes for the fork except in this case it would be a man. I do not believe in the superstition, nor do I believe that any of my family does, but I have in fact announced the arrival of the particular gender when the appropriate utensil dropped. The purpose of announcing the superstition even though one does not believe in it serves to pass on the tradition but also is a source of humor. I have even passed it on to my roommates who think it’s funny too.
